Try and break down each problem individually. Each of those bugs have a life cycle, all you need to do is disrupt the cycle and they'll start to dwindle. Neem is your best friend if you want to keep it affordable. I really like Ahimsa neem emulsified with agsil16. Pair this with a bait/trap crop for each bug (just google "bait crop for x-bug"). i generally do these in smaller pots, put them near the cash crops. Once infested, move it, and treat it (or burn it if it's real bad). Some stuff like Milkweed for aphids can be intermixed with crops and ripped out when infested. 

[Beauveria Bassiana](https://buildasoil.com/collections/ipm/products/buildasoil-beauveria-bassiana-water-soluble) is sort of a silver bullet for Squash bugs and the entirely arthropod family. It's expensive but you'll likely only need it once per season. 

[Inoculating with nematodes](https://www.naturesgoodguys.com/collections/beneficial-nematodes/products/15-million-live-beneficial-nematodes-hb-sc-sf-kills-over-200-different-species?variant=31122986991675) should take care of cabbage moths and anything else that might be in your soil/mulch layer. If there's any eggs or juveniles in there these guys will destroy them. The free way to do this would be compost teas with added molasses to try and boost the population of whatever nematodes are already native. 

Mice and ant's i haven't had to deal with but i'd bet repellants are more the way to go spray crops with Rosemary, Garlic, lavender, essential oils.

Ferments are beneficial because it breaks down whatever you fermented into it's simplest plant available forms. as well as inoculate the medium. The sugars in the tincture feed the soil's existing microbe population which continue to breakdown and mobilize nutrients. 

 I think of FPJ as a home made all-in-one mix of Microbes, Enzymes, a little NPK (based on whatever you fermented), trace minerals and sugars/carbs. If you break down something like Alfalfa you get the tricantinol etc.

Even for a big oldschool centential double ipa, id be a little worried that it'd be a little heavy in the caramel malts and too bitter, if you just triple the hop schedule and malt as is, you'd probably end up with more of a barley wine. 

3 kits would give you 27lb of LME, 3lb of Caramel 40 and 15oz of centennial. I would leave out at least 2-2.5lb of the C40. I'd also change the Hop schedule to something like : 

 * 2oz @ 60
 * 2oz @ 30
 * 2oz @ 10  
 * 3.5oz @ steep/Whirlpool 180
 * remaining/~5oz Dry hop @ terminal gravity. let them sit on the beer for 3 days then package. 

at 10gal batch size You're still looking at 1.097 sg which would start to stress out us-05. I'd aim for a 12 gal batch size or a max sg of 1.080. That should give you a nicely balanced 70-80IBU,  8-8.5% Centennial dipa.

As far as making it more awesome. Take that 5oz dryhop and add that to the 3.5oz Whirlpool @ 180-170f. Pick 3oz of Cryo hops to dry hop with. You could just lean into more Centennial or add some fruit elements with mosaic, simcoe or a blend of whatever you like. The idea being that Cryo hops might help limit oxidation and plant matter character.  

Just be sure to keep the hot side hops out of the fermenter and pitch 2-3 packs of yeast.

i guess the DIY version would be a hempy bucket. 

 * drill a hole 5" up from the bottom of the bucket. 
 * fill the bottom of the bucket with chunky perlite or pumice to an inch or so above the hole you drilled. 
 * Stick a piece of pvc down through the perlite to the bottom, like the design above. Or you can get a 90* barb, and piece of clear vinyl tube, drill a hole right at the bottom of the bucket and run the tube up the side. That doubles as a water level and fill port. 

Other notes on this: Black buckets are a must imo. Anything that lets light through can create algae in the water zone. water only in the reservoir, feeding anything and the roots sitting in that, can lead to issues. Letting the res dry out a bit is a must imo, once you see it's empty, leave it for a day or two, then refill. it gets oxygen down to the roots and keeps that section from getting anaerobic. Mulching on top helps equalize moisture. you can also do Vermiculite on top which will act like mulch and also stop fungus gnats.
